📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, raised beds are cosy homes for vegetables, annuals and perennials, but, like all homes, they require maintenance. When you prepare raised beds for winter, you make things easier for all your plants next season. With proper care, you can ensure that your raised bed frames and soils are safe from frost and winter rain, and that any plants you subsequently add can hit the ground running.

Because raised beds sit above the ground, their soil cools down faster, is more exposed to biting winter wind, and faces heavier nutrient leaching from seasonal downpours. Neglected beds may develop drainage issues or lose valuable nutrients. The best raised garden bed ideas protect your soil from winter’s worst. Taking a few simple winter-smart steps now can help to extend the life of the soil, prevent nutrient leaching, and make a strong spring harvest far more likely.

Sources indicate that best of all, these winterizing tasks are quick, low-effort wins. Whether you are tending a single cedar herb box or galvanized steel troughs, prepping your beds now guarantees more fertile soil in spring, earlier planting windows, healthier perennials, and your most bountiful harvests yet. Here’s how to protect your raised beds through winter.

Recent findings suggest that before you start these tasks, take a quick inventory of your raised bed setup. Size, depth, and construction material can all influence how your beds weather the cold. Wooden beds (like cedar, redwood, or pine) offer natural insulation, but absorb moisture, making them prone to swelling, warping, or fungal rot if soggy debris sits against the boards all winter. You can buy a wood sealant to protect bed frames from winter moisture, as long as it is safe, such as Seal It Green’s Plant-Based Garden Bed Sealer, available from Amazon.

Galvanized metal beds and stone beds are virtually rot-proof, but they conduct cold rapidly. This can mean that soil near the outer walls might freeze and thaw faster, putting perimeter plant roots under extra stress. Shallow beds under 10 inches (25cm) deep can also freeze solid much sooner than deep 18-24-inch (45-60cm) troughs. Bear all this in mind when tackling the jobs here.

Recent findings suggest that where you live has a part to play, too. In northern regions (USDA hardiness zones 3-6), you need to complete winter prep before the top few inches of soil freeze solid, typically by late November. In milder southern and coastal areas (zones 7-10), winterizing is more about suppressing cool-season weeds, preventing heavy rain from washing away nutrients, and tucking in cold-hardy crops like garlic or kale.

According to recent reports, visit your beds after rainfall to check soil moisture and drainage before beginning your winter tune-up. You can buy a soil temperature and moisture diagnostic tool, such as the Daybetter Soil Meter 4-in-1 from Walmart, to check whether raised bed soil is ready for cover crops or mulch. Then you are ready to get your beds in shape with these tips….

It used to be standard advice to strip beds bare in fall, but leaving soil naked can expose it to erosion, deplete soil nutrition, and destroy vital overwintering habitats for beneficial pollinators and predatory beetles. Instead, be selective about cleanup. Pull out all spent annual veg and frost-blackened fruiting crops such as tomatoes, peppers, and squash. Also remove persistent weeds. Don’t toss these into the compost pile, but bag them for municipal green waste.

For healthy, disease-free annuals like beans, peas, or marigolds, snip stems at soil level with clean pruners such as the Felco F2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon. Leaving the roots in the ground prevents soil disturbance and feeds earthworms and soil microbes as they decompose over winter. Finally, remove bamboo stakes, tomato cages, and trellises, scrubbing off clinging soil and fungal spores with a mild diluted bleach or vinegar wash before storing them dry.

It has been revealed that intensive raised bed gardening draws heavily on soil reserves over summer, leaving it depleted by November. Replenishing fertility now allows rain, snow, and microbial activity to work on amendments before spring planting begins. Gently loosen any compacted soil using a broadfork or standard garden fork. Push the tines in and rock back slightly. If you need a good fork, the Ames 4-Tine Forged Spading Fork from The Home Depot can help improve drainage without churning up soil structure.

In a recent development, spread a generous 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of aged organic compost, leaf mold, or well-rotted manure across the surface. Avoid hot, uncomposted manure, which can burn roots and leach excess nitrates. If your soil test indicates low phosphorus or acidity (common in high-rainfall regions) then add slow-acting mineral amendments such as rock phosphate, greensand, or garden lime. These require several months to break down and adjust soil chemistry before spring crops go in.

Industry observers note that once your soil is fed, your next mission is to protect the surface from winter erosion, temperature swings, and nutrient washout. Your first option is to tuck the soil under a thick blanket of fluffy organic mulch. For beds lying fallow, or housing perennial herbs and cold-hardy greens, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of shredded fall leaves, clean weed-free straw, or pine needles over your compost layer. Avoid heavy mats of wet grass clippings or unshredded oak leaves, which block oxygen and harbor slugs.

Alternatively, in mild regions, you can sow fast-establishing cover crops like winter rye, crimson clover, hairy vetch, or tillage daikon radish. Their roots help to anchor soil against torrential rain. They also scavenge leftover nitrogen and break up deep compaction, ready to be chopped down and turned 3-4 weeks before spring planting. Buy Outside Pride Crimson Clover Seeds from Amazon for just a few dollars.

Industry observers note that shallow-rooted perennials and newly planted spring bulbs in raised beds face a couple of threats: frost heaving and hungry digging pests. Repeated freezing nights and thawing sunny days can cause wet soil to expand and contract, pushing shallow crowns such as coral bells, foamflowers, and strawberries out of the earth. To prevent frost heave, wait until the ground has frozen lightly. Then mound 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of shredded leaves or evergreen boughs around the crowns. This locks in consistent cold temperatures rather than trapping warmth that delays dormancy.

Raised beds packed with newly planted tulips, crocus, or ranunculus bulbs are very tempting for squirrels, voles, and chipmunks. Lay half-inch hardware cloth or chicken wire flat across the soil surface, weighing down the edges with bricks or landscape staples. If you need a good mesh then Ashman Online Hardware Cloth, available from The Home Depot, can stop squirrels and voles from digging up bulbs. Remove it in early spring as green shoots emerge.

Industry observers note that winter can put structural stress on raised beds, making this the ideal time for a quick inspection. Walk the perimeter and check corner brackets, screws, and timber boards for splitting, wood rot, or rust. Tighten any loose hardware and brace any bowing sides, especially on long wooden beds over 8 feet (2.4m) long. Place a spirit level across the top edges to ensure frames haven't settled unevenly. You can buy Allfun Metal Raised Bed Brackets from Amazon to reinforce ageing or bowing wooden bed corners.

According to recent reports, inspect drainage after heavy rain. Note whether the water pools, where it pools, and how rapidly it clears up. Well-draining soil should clear water within 15-20 minutes. If puddles linger, check whether landscape fabric or cardboard at the base has clogged with silt, and use a garden fork to punch deep drainage channels into the subsoil. Finally, check soil height. Ideally, the soil needs to sit 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) below the top rim. Top up sunken beds with a 50/50 blend of topsoil and compost.

If your raised beds house overwintering crops or borderline-hardy perennials, adding some protection can extend harvests and save tender specimens from icy blasts. Because raised beds warm up faster than surrounding ground, they respond well to low tunnels and protective covers. For grafted roses in deep raised beds, mound 6-10 inches (15-25cm) of compost, aged bark, straw or soil over the graft union.

Industry observers note that for tender perennials, drape medium-weight breathable horticultural fleece (frost cloth) over flexible PVC or wire hoops anchored into the inside edges of the bed frame. For a breathable winter frost blanket, you can buy AGFabric Floating Row Covers from Walmart to shield overwintering veg and tender perennials, while allowing light and moisture through. Secure edges with spring clamps so that winter gales don’t whip covers away. Another good option is a straw-filled wire cage.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

Long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat. His name was Stubby, and by the time the First World War ended, he had become the most decorated dog in American military history.

Sources indicate that stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in Upcoming Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France. A short-tailed, brindle-colored dog of uncertain breeding, likely part Boston terrier and part American bull terrier, wandered into camp and was adopted by Private J. Robert Conroy. Soldiers were not permitted to keep pets, but Stubby won over the men, and eventually the officers, by learning to mimic military customs. He reportedly marched in step with the troops and raised a paw to his brow in a passable salute.

Recent findings suggest that when the 102nd Infantry shipped out for France, the transport ships barred dogs. Conroy smuggled Stubby aboard the SS Minnesota hidden beneath his overcoat. Conroyâs commanding officer discovered Stubby during the crossing, but his salute reportedly charmed the officer into letting him stay.

Recent findings suggest that once in France, Stubbyâs role shifted from morale booster to something closer to that of a working soldier. He entered combat on February 5, 1918, at Chemin des Dames, enduring shelling for over a month, and went on to serve through 17 battles over 18 months on the Western Front.

After surviving a mustard gas attack, Stubby developed a heightened sensitivity to the smell of gas. Historians and contemporary newspaper accounts credit him with warning his regiment of subsequent gas attacks before the men could detect it themselves. This allowed soldiers time to don their masks. He was also credited with locating wounded soldiers in no manâs land and comforting them until stretcher bearers arrived.

Recent findings suggest that stubbyâs most famous exploit occurred when he discovered a German soldier mapping the layout of Allied trenches. According to accounts preserved by military historians, Stubby seized the man until American soldiers arrived to take him prisoner. For this act, Stubby was informally promoted to the rank of sergeant, making him, according to most accounts, the first dog to receive a rank in the United States Armed Forces. This was, of course, an honorary and unofficial designation rather than a formal commission, since the military does not commission dogs.

Industry observers note that during the April 1918 German offensive on the town of Seicheprey, France, Stubby was wounded in the chest and leg by grenade shrapnel while accompanying the 102nd Infantry in combat. After recovering, he returned to visiting wounded soldiers in the hospital, walking the wards to lift the spirits of recovering men.

Sources indicate that stubby returned home a celebrity. He led parades, attended war bond rallies, and met three sitting or future presidents: Woodrow Wilson, Warren G. Harding, and Calvin Coolidge. General John J. Pershing personally honored him at a 1921 ceremony for the 102nd Infantry Regiment, presenting him with a gold medal from the Humane Education Society, an award that, while not an official military commendation, cemented his reputation as the greatest war dog of his era.

According to recent reports, conroy went on to attend Georgetown University Law Center, and Stubby went with him, becoming the unofficial mascot of the Georgetown Hoyas football team. At halftime, he would nudge a football around the field to the delight of the crowd.

According to recent reports, stubby died in 1929, reportedly in Conroyâs arms. His remains were preserved and are held today by the Smithsonianâs National Museum of American History, where he wears the medals and blanket he wore during his years of service. In 2018, an animated film called Sgt. Stubby: An American Hero introduced his story to a upcoming generation. That same year, the descendants of Conroy dedicated a life-sized bronze statue of him at the Connecticut Trees of Honor Memorial in Middletown, Connecticut.

Stubby served nearly a quarter century before the United States Army established a formal War Dog Program in 1942. He had no training pipeline, no breeding program, and no structure to recognize what he did. He was, in the truest sense, an amateur who became indispensable through instinct, loyalty, and repeated exposure to danger alongside the men who fed and sheltered him. Later advocates of formal military working dog programs often cite his legacy as early proof of concept: a dogâs senses, courage, and bond with a handler could save human lives on a modern battlefield.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

In a recent development, support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Sources indicate that keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

In a recent development, follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

It has been revealed that if Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Tech Report: 6 Plants That Need Mulching in November to Keep Roots Cozy as Temperatures Fall – and 4 You Should Never Cover

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that late fall is an crucial time to prep a garden for winter, and knowing which plants to mulch in November is a vital part of the blueprint. As weather worsens and the ground begins to freeze, adding an insulating layer of mulch keeps soil temperatures more stable, helping plants to survive winter better. Protected from freeze-thaw cycles, frost heaving and low temperatures that could cause root damage, mulched plants will wake up in spring ready for abundant growth.

In a recent development, because many plants have died down by late fall, mulching in November is a speedy and satisfying job on a crisp sunny day. All you need to do is spread a layer of mulch on top of the soil, keeping it away from the plant stems, which is easy with a hand rake such as this from Lowe's. For best results, choose a mulch made of natural materials like compost, shredded leaves or bark, as it will start breaking down over the winter to supply the soil with nutrients, ready to fuel that strong spring growth.

Many folk like to mulch all their borders when winterizing a garden in fall because it not only protects plants but helps to suppress weeds and keeps beds looking smart over winter. However, while most plants will get through winter better if treated to a fall mulch, there are a few which don't appreciate this extra layer so it's vital to know which to leave be. There are a few plants that seriously benefit from a late fall mulch, too, so even if you're not planning on protecting your whole yard, it's well worth mulching these garden heroes. Here's everything you need to know to get great results.

If you’ve planted new perennials this fall, whether you bought them from a garden center or had success creating free plants by dividing your perennials, they're likely not fully established in their new home yet. This means they're more vulnerable than your other perennials to the cold temperatures and fluctuations of winter weather.

It has been revealed that mulching now is a smart idea for all newly planted perennials, but especially any that are borderline hardy in your growing region. Loosely apply three to four inches (8-10cm) of mulch around these plants as the soil begins to freeze.

Many roses benefit from winter mulching, especially less hardy varieties and those that are newly planted. Fluctuating temperatures can damage plants and cause frost heaving, pushing the roots out of the ground. Mulch roses with 8 to 12 inches (20-30cm) of compost or organic mulch, or even loose, light soil around their bases, keeping the mulching material a couple inches away from the stems of the plants to prevent moisture collection that can trigger rot.

Reliably hardy, well-established hydrangeas may not need mulching but younger plants will benefit from a protective layer this month. Hydrangeas have shallow roots that can be damaged by the cold and the frost heaving that often results from freeze-thaw cycles. Winter damage can stunt spring growth, so a layer of mulch can give your plants a head start next season.

Mulch hydrangeas with two to six inches (5-15cm) of organic material, depending on how cold your winters are. Keep in mind that mulch only protects the roots, so you may also want to protect buds growing on old wood with a burlap wrap during cold snaps.

It has been revealed that your spring bulbs – tulips, crocuses, daffodils and hyacinths – need time to establish roots before winter, and fluctuating soil temperatures can disrupt this process by freezing and thawing repeatedly. The solution is to apply two to three inches of light, loose mulch as the soil begins to freeze. This keeps soil temperatures more consistent, and can also prevent premature emergence during periods of milder winter weather.

If you're adding spring-flowering bulbs that can still be planted in November to your garden – and there are plenty that are fine to go into the soil this late in fall – then mulch straight after planting.

Strawberries are particularly vulnerable to damage caused by cold temperatures but also by the cycles of freezing and thawing that many gardens experience. Cover your strawberry patch with a loose layer of three to four inches of an organic mulch. Weed-free straw such as HealthiStraw GardenStraw, available from Amazon, is a good choice for protecting without compacting and weighing down delicate strawberry plants. Pull the straw back in spring as you see upcoming growth, but leave it around the edges or between rows of plants to keep berries clean and off the ground as they develop.

While many people use mums as fall annuals, there are hardy chrysanthemums that can be grown as perennials with the right care. To get them to come back next year, though, you’ll need to add some mulch for winter protection. They have shallow roots, so the extra insulation helps prevent cold damage. To protect your upcoming garden mums, leave the foliage intact and spread a loose layer of a few inches of organic mulch under and around the leaves.

Always choose a mulch made from natural plant materials, as that will improve your soil as well as protect your plants. Choose undyed mulch to avoid adding unnecessary chemicals to the soil, and there's no need to use mulch binder or glue to keep it in place.

You can buy purpose-made mulch like like Timberline Pine Bark Mulch, stocked by Lowe's, but there are plenty of other options to choose from to suit your garden style and budget. You could use homemade compost or a store-bought compost like Back to the Roots Organic Compost, available from Amazon. Fall leaves that you've shredded by running the lawn mower over a few times make an excellent, free mulch, while bark chips like Golden Trophy Pine Bark Nuggets from Walmartadd texture to your beds.

Recent findings suggest that coco coir chips such as Riare Organic Coco Husk Chips, available from Amazon, are a sustainable option as they're made from outer coconut husks, are a sustainable option. Because they're packaged in a dehydrated form, the bales are compact and light to carry. While coco coir is a very effective mulch, it's not the best option for an exposed garden as after a long dry spell the chips can become light enough to be blown around by strong winds.

All these natural mulches will break down to enrich your soil and improve its structure so it drains freely yet holds onto valuable moisture.

November is the right time to mulch in many gardens, but it’s important to follow your local conditions when deciding on exact timing, depending on your USDA zone. Applying mulch early might feel like you’re getting ahead, but this can warm the soil too much and delay plants going into dormancy. So, wait until plants are dormant and the ground is beginning to freeze, which typically happens after several hard frosts.

In a recent development, for all the plants that will thank you for the cozy winter coverage mulch provides, a few can be damaged by it. These plants are vulnerable to excessive moisture, poor airflow, or having their crowns and growth points covered so, while they may benefit from a very light layer of mulch, be careful not to smother them.

Winter mulching is all about strategic protection, not simply covering everything in a thick layer of insulation. But get it right and employ a few insulating frost jackets to zip up vulnerable plants and keep them cozy, and your garden will be protected from the worst of the winter cold, ready to flourish once spring arrives.

My cat, Mitzi, is 16 years and 8 months old. She has early-stage kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, which she is on medication for. About 2 months ago, she became deaf, and since then has refused to leave the master bedroom. I have moved her water bowl and litter box there and feed her there.

Is there anything I can do to get her to come out?â.

It has been revealed that at her age, sweet Mitzi has certainly earned the right to enjoy her golden years at her own pace, but I can imagine it is difficult to see her withdraw from the rest of the house, especially when you remember how she used to move around. However, I would not necessarily interpret her reluctance to leave the bedroom as something we need to correct. Losing her hearing can be quite disorienting. Imagine walking into a room where you can no longer hear footsteps, familiar voices, or the little sounds that help you understand what is happening around you. For Mitzi, the bedroom may now feel like her safest little world, where everything is familiar and predictable.

In a recent development, I actually think you have done a wonderful job adapting her environment by bringing her food, water, and litter box closer. Rather than encouraging her to leave right away, I would focus on helping her feel confident enough to explore if she wishes. You could start by sitting with her near the bedroom doorway, offering a favorite treat or a little affection. Gradually place treats a short distance beyond the door, allowing her to decide whether she wants to investigate.

In a recent development, take care to only approach her within her visual field, avoid startling her while she sleeps, and keep pathways clear and nonslip. Think of it as extending her new world one comfortable step at a time, rather than asking her to return to her old routine.

Recent findings suggest that there is one thing I would not overlook, though. Mitzi has both chronic kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, and at her age, reduced mobility or withdrawal can also be associated with arthritis, high blood pressure, visual changes, or inadequate control of her thyroid disease. I would recommend a senior cat veterinary checkup that includes blood pressure measurement, assessment for arthritis, and follow-up kidney and thyroid testing. Sometimes what looks like a behavioral change is actually a senior cat quietly telling us that they are in pain and something does not feel quite right.

Most importantly, please do not feel that you are encouraging a bad habit by keeping her essentials in the bedroom. You are adapting her home to meet her changing needs, and that is a beautiful expression of your love and care for her. If the bedroom is where Mitzi feels safe, eats well, drinks, uses her litter box, and enjoys your company, that can be a perfectly good quality of life.

At this stage, happiness is not measured by how much of the house she explores, but by how comfortable and secure she feels in the little world she chooses.

I have a question about my dog, Jethro. Sometimes when he alerts, the hackles between his shoulders rise. Other times they are prominent along his lower back. What does each appearance indicate about how he is responding?â.

Industry observers note that that is a great observation! When a dogâs hackles rise, it is an involuntary response controlled by the autonomic nervous system called piloerection, and it tells us that his arousal level has increased. However, the location of the raised hair does not reliably tell us which emotion a dog is experiencing.

In a recent development, when the hackles rise between his shoulders, it can accompany alertness, excitement, uncertainty, or concern. When they appear along his lower back, the same range of emotional responses is possible. Neither pattern automatically indicates aggression, fear, or a particular level of threat. Think of hackles as a little emotional alarm bell; they tell us Jethro is experiencing heightened arousal, but not exactly why.

Different dogs will respond to different stimuli in different ways, so thereâs no âone size fits allâ explanation for why different areas are triggered. I would pay close attention to what is happening around him when this occurs. Is he alerting to a stranger approaching the house, another dog walking past, an unfamiliar noise, or something unexpected in the environment? You might want to start keeping a record of what is going on before and after Jethroâs hackles are raised, and whether itâs his shoulders or lower back that is involved.

According to recent reports, combine that context with his facial expression, ear position, tail carriage, posture, muscle tension, and ability to disengage. Looking at the whole picture helps us understand whether Jethro is curious, excited, uncertain, or uncomfortable, and, most importantly, how we can best support him. These details, together with what triggered the alert, give us a much clearer picture of how Jethro is feeling.

These 8 Evergreen Plants Make Your Porch Look Magical at Christmas – And They Stay Gorgeous All Winter

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight. Yet when chosen thoughtfully, they can become show-stopping centerpieces. This is a time of year to celebrate the holiday season, but rather than relying on temporary displays, why not go for something with real staying power?

Growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter. Flanking a front door or framing porch steps with holiday porch pots filled with living potted evergreens offers charm and longevity. Beyond classic deep emerald needles, today’s best container evergreens can deliver winter berries, flowers, contrasting textures, and even fragrance to greet guests as they arrive at your stoop.

According to recent reports, best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down. With minimal upkeep, they lend easy elegance through the dark days of winter, then you can move them as needed to assist in decades-long displays. From trailing options to compact shrubs, here are 8 gorgeous evergreens you can use to transform your front porch into an enchanting holiday welcome.

Growing evergreens in containers unlocks wonderful design flexibility, allowing you to cluster different heights, trailing textures, and berry accents right at eye level near your doorway. However, while container-grown evergreens are generally easygoing and make great seasonal décor, they need a little more winter care than evergreens growing in the ground.

Industry observers note that because their potted roots sit above ground, they are more vulnerable to freezing temperatures and drying winter winds. It’s a good idea to choose evergreen varieties that are rated at least one or two USDA hardiness zones colder than your local climate, so plant roots have the best shot at surviving winter freezes unscathed.

Use frost-proof containers crafted from thick resin, fiberglass, glazed stoneware, or heavy wood. Avoid unglazed thin terracotta in cold climates, as trapped moisture will expand and crack clay walls. If your winters are very cold, consider wrapping the pots in burlap. Always leave unobstructed drainage holes and elevate your pots slightly on pot feet so icy water doesn't have a chance to pool underneath. You can buy Tortoise Pot Toes from Amazon to help ensure the best drainage.

Fill the containers with a coarse, fast-draining potting mix. Once you are past the holiday season and heading to spring, you can add a slow-release organic fertilizer. Even in winter, evergreens continue losing moisture through their foliage. Check the soil every couple of weeks and water deeply whenever the top two inches (5cm) feel dry and temperatures are above freezing. You’re now ready to add some of these evergreens to make your porch sparkle during Christmas and shine all winter long….

Alberta spruce is a classic choice for a Christmas tree, but most are large. If you fancy flanking your front door with classic, miniature Christmas trees, dwarf Alberta spruce (Picea glauca ‘Conica’) is perfect for a pot. Hardy across zones 3-8, this conifer naturally grows into a dense, velvety green, symmetrical cone, so it requires zero shearing to maintain its crisp silhouette. Also, because it adds just 2-4 inches (5-10cm) of growth per year, it thrives in a generous 14-18-inch (35-45cm) container for years, before needing upsizing or transplanting into the yard.

Place in full sun to light afternoon shade, rotating every few weeks. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but sharply drained, and mist occasionally. For a little extra holiday magic, underplant with trailing wintergreen or variegated ivy. Avoid heavy ornaments that might bend the fine branch tips. You can buy Dwarf Alberta Spruce from Nature Hills at a 30% discount. Add a couple for a lovely, symmetrical entryway feature.

Boxwood (Buxus spp.) brings classic English-garden elegance to winter porches in zones 5-9. Its dense clusters of small, glossy leaves stay green through sub-freezing weather. For containers, choose compact, cold-hardy cultivars such as Green Velvet (which forms a lush, rounded mound) or Green Gem. You can buy Brighter Blooms Green Velvet Boxwood from Walmart. Alternatively, go for pre-trained pyramid and globe topiaries for instant architectural polish.

According to recent reports, place potted boxwoods in partial shade to full sun. In northern zones, shelter them from harsh afternoon winter sun and drying winds. Plant in well-drained potting soil, and water deeply when unfrozen soil dries out. Dress for the holidays with velvet ribbon bows or tuck crimson winterberry stems into the soil around the base. Save any light shaping shears for late spring after the risk of last frost is passed.

According to recent reports, nothing announces the arrival of Christmas quite like holly (Ilex spp.), with its glossy leaves and scarlet berries. While towering tree hollies quickly outgrow porch pots, compact shrub cultivars thrive in containers in zones 5-9. Look for dwarf selections such as Little Red or compact Japanese Helleri. Alternatively, try deciduous winterberry Berry Poppins. Buy Proven Winners Berry Poppins Winterberry Holly from Plant Addicts for a container-sized beauty loaded with vibrant berry clusters.

Just remember that hollies are dioecious. To enjoy berries, you need a female cultivar paired near a compatible male (such as Mr Poppins for winterberry). Failing that, buy a nursery pot where both sexes are planted together. Grow hollies in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic potting mix. Keep berries safely out of reach of pets, and enjoy watching winter songbirds visit as spring approaches.

It has been revealed that if your front porch sits beneath a deep overhang or faces north where sun-loving conifers struggle, Japanese skimmia (Skimmia japonica) is a revelation. Hardy in zones 6-8, this neat, mounded broadleaf evergreen thrives in partial to full shade, retaining leathery, aromatic leaves all year. Better still, it delivers multi-season magic: in fall and early winter, male cultivars like Rubella produce clusters of flower buds that last right through Christmas, before opening into fragrant spring blossoms, while female varieties like Reevesiana bear true red berries.

According to recent reports, plant skimmia in an acidic, humus-rich potting mix (such as an ericaceous blend) with sharp drainage. Water regularly during dry spells, using rainwater if your tap water is hard. Nestle pots in a sheltered porch corner that is protected from icy gales. You can buy Skimmia Male Plants from Plant Addicts for shade-loving beauty to bedazzle on a covered porch. Add pinecones and ribbons to make pots festive.

Recent findings suggest that also known as eastern teaberry or boxberry, American wintergreen (Gaultheria procumbens) is a low-growing native evergreen groundcover. But it punches above its compact 6-inch (15cm) height in winter containers. Hardy in zones 3-8, its shiny, oval leaves transform over winter, from deep green to mahogany-bronze in cold weather. This provides a gorgeous backdrop for large, glossy red berries that cling to the stems all winter long.

In a recent development, because it trails gracefully over pot rims, it makes a lovely festive spiller around the base of dwarf spruce, boxwood, or winterberry stems in mixed holiday planters. Give it a spot in partial to full shade. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic potting soil. Keep soil consistently damp and avoid lime-heavy fertilizers. You can buy Arbor Day Foundation Store’s Wintergreen Teaberry Pot Plants from Amazon in triple packs. Perfect under a porch cover, awning, or larger tree or shrub.

Goldcrest cypress aka Goldcrest Monterey cypress (Hesperocyparis macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’) is also sold as lemon cypress, and it lives up to its names in winter porches. Hardy in zones 7-10 (and also enjoyed as a cool-room or sheltered patio container specimen in colder zones), this upright conifer is filled with chartreuse-gold foliage that releases a zesty aroma when you brush past it. You can buy Wonderland Flora’s Lemon Cypress Goldcrest Wilma Plants from Walmart in packs of four.

Its narrow, columnar shape fits neatly into tight entryway corners and pairs symmetrically beside front doors. Grow Goldcrest in full sun to intensify its golden hues, and plant in a fast-draining potting mix. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, but don’t let roots sit in soggy saucers. Dress the pot base with pinecones and burgundy ribbon for a contemporary holiday look that keeps sparkling into spring.

If you need to soften the edges of a structured winter pot, add some cascading English ivy (Hedera helix). Hardy in zones 4-9, this classic vining evergreen offers lobed emerald or crisp cream-and-gold variegations. Try cultivars like Glacier and Goldchild to brighten shady entryways with ease. While it can be invasive in the ground, it thrives in containers. Plant around the lip of mixed planters with upright boxwood or red-berried skimmia, or train up a wire obelisk for vertical interest.

According to recent reports, ivy thrives in partial to full shade, and prefers slightly drier, well-drained potting soil. Overwatering in winter is the main enemy. Just snip stray runners occasionally to keep trails tidy, and never allow stems to root into surrounding masonry. You can buy Glacier Ivy from Plant Addicts for trailing creams and greens to add lush, lively winter movement.

According to recent reports, if you want guests to pause in delight at your front door, plant sweet box (Sarcococca confusa). Hardy in zones 6-9, this understated, slow-growing broadleaf evergreen features dense, pointed leaves that look refined all year. What makes it unique for holiday decorating is that it flowers in winter. Depending on where you garden, you’ll have either buds or open flowers on this evergreen shrub at Christmas time. As a bonus, these creamy flowers are sweetly fragrant even on chilly days.

It has been revealed that sweet box thrives in deep to partial shade and prefers shelter from winds, so a covered front porch or courtyard alcove is ideal. Plant in a medium-sized container filled with rich, well-drained, neutral-to-slightly-acidic potting mix. Keep soil evenly moist when unfrozen. Minimal pruning is required: simply snip a few fragrant sprigs to tuck into holiday vases. You can buy Hirt’s Gardens Sweet & Lo Sweet Box Plants from Amazon for a shade-loving evergreen that fills entryways with honey scent.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Sources indicate that every time the topic of vaccines comes up, thereâs always someone who questions whether our pets really need them. Asking questions about medical care is perfectly reasonable (in fact, informed pet parents should!), but dismissing vaccination without understanding the risks is another story.

Rabies is a perfect example. This is not some historical disease or something that only affects animals in remote areas or underdeveloped countries. It can infect mammals, including our own cats, dogs, and even us. Whatâs even scarier is that once the clinical signs appear, rabies is almost always fatal, making prevention essential.

According to recent reports, recent events in Quebec offer a timely reminder. Amid an emerging wildlife outbreak, three domestic cats tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies in 2026. Although these numbers pale in comparison to the number of infected wildlife recorded since December 20241, it demonstrates how a disease circulating in wild animals can reach our pets.

And this isn't just a Canadian concern. Rabies variants and wildlife risks differ by region, but keeping pets appropriately vaccinated is a responsibility shared by pet parents everywhere.

It has been revealed that despite its name, raccoon-strain rabies isn't exclusive to raccoons; they are simply the reservoir species of this particular variant of the rabies virus. Skunks and other mammals â including cats â can also become infected.

Rabies attacks the central nervous system. It spreads mainly through the bite of an infected animal, when virus-containing saliva enters the body. Saliva can also transmit the virus if it reaches an open wound, the eyes, nose, or mouth.

Recent findings suggest that raccoon rabies had been eliminated in Quebec following an outbreak between 2006 and 2009, but the virus resurfaced in 2024. Since then, more outbreaks have appeared, and case numbers have climbed sharply in 2026, particularly in MontÃ©rÃ©gie. By October 29, 328 animals had tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies across the province. The three infected cats are examples of how a virus circulating in wildlife can also reach our pets, even though cats are not the main reservoir responsible for spreading this variant.

In a recent development, cats are naturally curious, territorial predators. They investigate unfamiliar scents, watch moving animals, explore hidden spaces, and sometimes pursue creatures that would be better left alone. These behaviors are normal expressions of feline biology, not evidence that a cat is being reckless.

Unfortunately, wildlife encounters can turn dangerous very quickly. A raccoon searching for food near a house may cross paths with an outdoor cat. A skunk hiding beneath a shed may be investigated by a curious feline. Even a sick or disoriented wild animal can catch a cat's attention, and one of the hallmarks of rabies infection in wild animals is a reduced fear of humans and predators as the infection attacks the nervous system. And cats being cats, curiosity can get them into trouble! These encounters don't just happen deep in the woods. A backyard, garage, or garden fence can be enough.

In a recent development, one of the infected cats was believed to have contracted rabies after contact with a wild animal. Another case led to three people receiving preventive treatment following possible exposure.

Rabies doesn't always turn an animal into a movie villain, either. Early signs can be subtle, which is why recognizing unusual behavior and reporting possible exposure is so important.

When people think of rabies, they often picture a snarling animal, dripping saliva, and attacking everything in sight. Hollywood certainly loves that version! Unfortunately, rabies doesn't always come with such obvious special effects.

In cats, the first signs can be surprisingly subtle. A normally friendly kitty may suddenly become grumpy, hide more than usual, vocalize differently, lose interest in food, or behave in ways that seem completely out of character. Since cats are already experts at keeping their humans guessing, a sudden behavior change can sometimes be easy to dismiss. But when a cat starts acting noticeably different from their usual, wonderfully weird self, it's worth paying attention.

As the disease progresses, neurological signs become more apparent. Affected cats may become disoriented, walk unsteadily, have difficulty swallowing, drool excessively, develop weakness, or eventually become paralyzed. Some become unusually aggressive or sensitive to touch, sounds, and light.

According to recent reports, there is also a less dramatic presentation called paralytic rabies, sometimes referred to as âdumb rabiesâ. Instead of becoming aggressive, affected animals may become unusually quiet, weak, or withdrawn. Difficulty swallowing, a drooping jaw, and progressive paralysis can follow. So no, a rabid animal doesn't necessarily look like it's auditioning for a horror movie.

In a recent development, of course, these signs can also occur with other neurological conditions, injuries, and intoxications. Nobody should attempt to diagnose rabies based on behavior alone. A cat showing sudden, unexplained neurological changes needs prompt veterinary attention, particularly if wildlife exposure is possible.

Sources indicate that here's another catch: rabies can take weeks, sometimes even months, to show itself. A cat may seem perfectly fine after an encounter with an infected animal, but that doesn't mean the virus isn't already in its body. So if a possible exposure happens, don't wait for your cat to look sick before calling the vet. By then, it may be too late.

Sadly, once rabies reaches the clinical stage, there is no cure, and the outcome is almost always fatal. That's why a suspected exposure should never be a wait-and-see situation. Don't wait for signs to appear; contact your veterinarian right away. With rabies, prevention isn't just better than treatment; it's our best chance to protect our cats in the first place.

In a recent development, think your indoor cat doesn't need a rabies vaccine? Think again! Indoor cats have fewer opportunities to encounter wildlife, but escapes happen, doors get left open, and sometimes wildlife finds its way indoors. Nobody prepares these little adventures, least of all the cat!

Industry observers note that rabies vaccination is also required by law for cats in many countries and jurisdictions. Even where it isn't mandatory, keeping your cat vaccinated is an crucial part of preventive care. Ask your veterinarian about the appropriate schedule for your cat.

And remember, vaccination doesn't mean ignoring a possible exposure. If your vaccinated cat is bitten by a potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian right away.

If your cat is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, contact your veterinarian immediately, even if your cat seems perfectly fine. Bite wounds can hide beneath all that lovely fur, and waiting for signs to appear is not an option.

Industry observers note that keep your cat away from other animals and don't try to catch or handle the wild animal. Report suspicious wildlife to local authorities and let trained professionals deal with it.

Recent findings suggest that if a person is bitten or scratched, or infected saliva enters an open wound or contacts the eyes, nose, or mouth, wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Post-exposure treatment can prevent rabies from developing, so don't delay.

Sources indicate that and please, leave dead wildlife alone. No bare-handed investigations or impromptu rescue missions!

Quebec is also fighting the outbreak through wildlife surveillance and vaccination campaigns using vaccine baits. These efforts help protect wild animals and reduce further spread.

Cats will be cats. A rustling bush can become the most fascinating thing in the universe, and a passing raccoon may look like an invitation to investigate. We can't blame them for being curious. We can give them safer ways to enjoy their adventures.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture a hose still screwed onto the spigot in December.
  • It's a fall chore, best done the same day you winterize sprinklers.
  • Recent findings suggest that outdoor faucet winterization is mostly about getting water out and keeping it from getting trapped again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture a hose still screwed onto the spigot in December. The water behind it has nowhere to go. Once nights stay below 32°F (0°C), it can freeze solid, and copper and brass don't have much give. Something splits. That repair bill usually runs well past what the faucet cost, so it pays to sort out how to winterize an outdoor faucet now.

It's a fall chore, best done the same day you winterize sprinklers. The annoying part is where the damage hides. From the yard, the faucet can look fine while the pipe behind it has cracked a few inches inside the wall. Nobody sees that until the water's back on.

Recent findings suggest that outdoor faucet winterization is mostly about getting water out and keeping it from getting trapped again. Take off the hose, shut off the supply, drain what's left, and add a cover for backup. Try to finish alongside your other gardening winterizing tasks, and before the first hard freeze reveals up in the forecast.

In a recent development, if you only get to one step today, make it this one. Any hose left on the spigot holds water inside the faucet, and that goes for frost-free models too – the water has nowhere to drain while the hose is attached. Splitters, watering timers, and quick-connect fittings trap water the same way, so pull them all off.

Then empty the hose. Stretch it down a slope or drape loops over a fence rail so the water runs out both ends. Leftover water can freeze and split it, and a drained hose stored out of the weather generally holds up longer. Suncast's 100-foot Hose Hideaway from Walmart keeps a coiled hose off the ground under a lid.

Start inside. Standard faucets usually have their own shutoff, somewhere close to where the pipe goes out through the wall, often in a basement, crawl space, or utility room. Look up between the ceiling joists, too. A round handle turns clockwise until it stops. If it's a lever, a quarter turn puts it crosswise to the pipe, and that's closed.

Not every home has one, and older houses often don't, which makes it harder to winterize hose bib lines without shutting off water to the whole house. If you're not sure what an unlabeled valve is, leave it alone. Close the wrong one, and it's no fun to find out halfway through washing dishes. Frost-free faucets, like this SharkBite one, work differently and may not need this step.

Sources indicate that for faucets without a dedicated indoor shutoff, a Freeze Miser outdoor faucet protector offers another option. It screws onto the spigot and automatically releases a small amount of water when the water temperature drops below 37°F (3°C), helping prevent freezing. Unlike conventional winterizing, this method requires leaving the water supply on and the outdoor faucet fully open.

Industry observers note that head back outside and open the faucet all the way. Some water should run out, slow to a trickle, and stop. Did it keep flowing? Then the indoor valve isn't closed all the way, or it's not the right valve at all.

According to recent reports, some shutoffs have a little cap on the side, called a bleeder. Leave the outdoor faucet open so air can get in, set a bucket underneath, and back the cap off slowly. Water will dribble out. When it quits, screw the cap back on. Many plumbers will leave the outdoor faucet open all winter. Some valve makers say to close it, though, so go by whatever came with yours.

An outdoor faucet cover holds in a little of the warmth that seeps through the wall from inside. The rigid type (like the image above) is a foam-lined dome with a cord that pulls it snug against the siding. Home Depot's Everbilt hard outdoor faucet cover is a good cheap option. Flexible pouches go on more like a sock (see image below), and the Thinsulate-lined faucet socks on Amazon come two to a pack.

Either kind should sit flat against the wall with no gap for cold air. Check it after windy nights, because covers do get knocked loose. It's backup, not a substitute for unhooking hoses and draining the line, and outdoor spigot winter protection still starts with an empty faucet. An Ambient Weather Wi-Fi weather station can send temperature alerts to your phone before a hard freeze.

Sources indicate that plenty of people hear frost-free and figure that means forget about it. That's about half right, maybe. From the yard, a frost-free outdoor faucet looks like any other spigot. Its handle turns a long stem, and the part that stops the water sits way back at the end of it, where it's warmer. Close it, and the water in that stem should run out the spout. That only works if the faucet slopes a little toward the outside.

Sources indicate that so the hose still comes off, or water stays put and can freeze inside the wall, often unnoticed until spring. Damage, a level installation, or a pipe running through an unheated crawl space can leave one vulnerable too.

Industry observers note that correctly installed ones usually don't need the supply shut off and drained, but the manufacturer's instructions get the final say. Homes without an indoor shutoff can have a plumber fit a replacement such as the SharkBite one mentioned above.

Sources indicate that if the faucet won't run or ice has formed around the spout, skip the torch, even if one happens to be sitting right there in the garage. No open flame, and nothing else that blasts heat at it, either. There's framing and insulation right behind that siding. Hair dryers are slower. Point it at the faucet and the wall around it and give it time. Keep the cord out of puddles.

In a recent development, suspect a leak? Shut off the water to that line, or the main valve if there's no separate one, and call a plumber. Frozen pipe damage isn't always visible right away. A crack of ⅛ inch (3 mm) can let out up to 250 gallons (946L) a day, and it may not drip at all until the ice thaws or the water goes back on.

Most of what it takes to protect outdoor faucets from freezing – and to prevent frozen pipes behind them – is getting the water out and keeping it out. Get that done before the first hard frost, and the faucet should be ready come spring, with dry walls behind it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Poinsettias might be the traditional choice for festive decorating, but they're not the only Christmas houseplants capable of bringing a splash of holiday color indoors.

If you're looking for something a little different this year, there is a holiday plant that promises the same bold red hues of a poinsettia, along with glossy succulent leaves and a surprisingly easygoing nature. And no, we're not talking about sweet box (although that's also a brilliant container plant to add to your shopping list).

Instead, we're dragging the beautiful Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) into the spotlight, as its flowers can last for weeks, making it a lovely way to brighten your home through the darker months.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Often sold as a seasonal flowering plant, Flaming Katy is actually a tender perennial succulent, which means you don't necessarily have to throw it away once Christmas is over. In fact, all you have to do is give it the right conditions and it can continue growing for years, potentially rewarding you with another spectacular display.

Recent findings suggest that there's no denying that poinsettias look impressive, but they can be surprisingly fussy about their surroundings, as they dislike cold draughts and sudden temperature changes – so much so that their leaves can drop. Overwatering is another common problem, particularly when plants are left sitting in decorative pots without adequate drainage.

Flaming Katy offers a much easier alternative, as its leaves store water, helping it cope with occasional dry spells, while its clusters of brightly colored flowers provide plenty of festive impact. Red is a particularly popular choice for Christmas, of course, although you can also find varieties with pink, orange, yellow and white flowers, too.

Industry observers note that better still? Rather than providing a brief burst of colour, a healthy plant can remain in bloom for several weeks, sometimes even longer depending on the variety and growing conditions.

It has been revealed that unlike some Christmas houseplants, this one doesn't need constant attention to keep looking good. Once you find a suitable position (a birght windowsill is ideal), the main thing is to avoid overwatering and make sure it receives enough light.

It also prefers average indoor humidity, so there's no need to mist it or create a particularly humid environment; in fact, good air circulation is more useful than excessive moisture around the leaves. Just keep it somewhere warm, ideally with temperatures around 60–75°F (16–24°C), and give it plenty of bright, indirect light (and remember that some gentle morning sunshine is generally welcome, too).

During the flowering period, you can remove individual faded flower clusters to keep the plant looking tidy, but there's no need for complicated pruning or constant feeding.

Perhaps the best thing about Flaming Katy is that, even though it's a Christmas houseplant, it doesn't have to be a disposable festive decoration; once flowering finishes, you can continue growing it as a foliage houseplant. With the right care, it can produce new growth and flower again.

According to recent reports, oh sure, poinsettias will always have their place in Christmas decorating, but Flaming Katy makes a convincing alternative if you'd prefer something colorful, undemanding and potentially longer-lasting when it comes to brightening up a home during winter. And unlike a certain fussy red plant that pops up everywhere in the holidays, this little flowering succulent really can stick around for years.

What Your Jade Plant Needs in November – 5 Easy Ways to Unlock Lush Growth and Good Fortune in the Newly introduced Year

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, shorter days mean weaker sunlight streaming through the glass, while central heating inevitably clicks on.
  • Luckily, protecting your jade now is oh-so-simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with its sculptural trunk, plump leaves, and reputation as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune, a healthy jade plant (Crassula ovata) can thrive for decades. Yet as November settles in, these plants quietly shift into semi-dormancy as less sun naturally fills the space. This can make a jade feel vulnerable if your care routine stays stuck in summer mode.

In a recent development, shorter days mean weaker sunlight streaming through the glass, while central heating inevitably clicks on. Stand beside a sunny windowsill in the afternoon and it can feel cozy, yet by evening an icy chill radiates off the pane. Because of this, your jade plant care routine needs to adapt. It would be foolish to water as you did months earlier, or leave a prized specimen pressed against a drafty sill. If you’re not careful, you might risk triggering leaf drop, soft stems, or weak and leggy growth.

Luckily, protecting your jade now is oh-so-simple. Just a few seasonal adjustments prevent calamity, so you can preserve those glossy, coin-shaped leaves, and even encourage delicate star-shaped winter blooms. And for anyone looking to boost their fortunes in the new year, it all starts here and now by giving your beloved jade plants the right care and attention. Here’s how to help yours thrive through winter, so it sees in spring in the very best shape.

In a recent development, jade plant care this month comes down to balancing your own comfort against your plant’s natural seasonal rhythm. While you turn up the thermostat and pull the curtains against the dark, your jade craves bright, crisp days, cool nights, and dry feet. Even innocently shifting a pot aside to make room for holiday decor can plunge your sun-loving succulent into stressful gloom or into the path of a radiator blast.

Industry observers note that your local climate and USDA hardiness zone still shape indoor care. In northern regions (zones 3-6), dry furnace air and frosty windowpanes pose the biggest threats. In mild coastal or southern regions (zones 9-11), anyone who risks keeping jades outdoors on patios must watch for cool rainstorms that might waterlog pots.

According to recent reports, before starting your tasks, clear any dust off the leaves with a soft brush so they absorb maximum winter light. If you fancy a closer look at your jade plant’s nooks and crannies, invest in a magnifying glass or a loupe, like the JarLink 30X 60X Illuminated Jeweler’s Loupe, available on Amazon. This can help you spot early mealybug fluff or scale bumps. It’s also a good idea to verify that drainage holes aren't blocked, before you start these essential jade care tasks.

Scaling back your watering routine is the single most impactful step you can take for a jade plant in November. As daylight dwindles and growth slows to a crawl, jade roots absorb moisture more slowly than they did in summer. Leaving roots sitting in a damp potting mix for weeks at a time invites fungal root rot. Before reaching for the watering can, push your index finger 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) down into the soil, insert a plain wooden chopstick to the bottom. Alternatively, use a probe like the inexpensive XLUX Plant Soil Moisture Meter from Amazon.

It has been revealed that if any dampness or dark soil clings to it, wait another week. When the mix is dry, water thoroughly until excess drains out the bottom hole. Empty the saucer immediately. Keep plant age and variety in mind. Compact varieties like Hobbit and Gollum, or young plants in small 4-inch (10cm) pots, dry out faster than massive specimens in deep tubs. Avoid over-correcting: if lower leaves feel thin, soft, or wrinkled, your jade plant is ready for a drink.

By November, the sun sits lower in the sky and a jade that did fine in an east or west window all summer may only catch a sliver of the light it needs now. Jade plants require at least 4-6 hours of bright, direct light daily to keep stems sturdy and leaves compact. This is especially true of variegated cultivars like Tricolor or Variegata, which have less chlorophyll and lose their creamy-pink margins in dim rooms. Relocate your jade to an unobstructed south-facing window or a bright west-facing sill. Make the move gradually over 3-4 days so leaves do not scorch.

Sources indicate that watch for early signs of light starvation, such as pale newly introduced leaves or elongated stems with wide gaps between leaf pairs (known as etiolation). If natural winter light falls short in northern latitudes, supplement with a full-spectrum LED grow bulb positioned 12-18 inches (30-45cm) above the canopy for 10-12 hours daily. Feit Electric's 9-Watt BR30 Medium E26 Full-Spectrum LED Grow Light Bulb from The Home Depot will screw into a plain old lamp socket. Switch your grow lights off at night, though. Uninterrupted dark, cool nights trigger mature jades to set flower buds.

Sources indicate that put your palm on the window glass one of these chilly mornings, and you'll know why the sill can be a rough spot. Jade has zero tolerance for frost or abrupt temperature shifts. Leaves pressed against a freezing pane can get damaged even indoors. Pull your potted jade back 3-6 inches (8-15cm) from cold windowpanes, and slide a piece of insulating cork or folded cloth beneath the pot on chilly stone or marble sills.

Recent findings suggest that also keep jades clear of exterior entry doors that blast icy air every time someone walks in, as well as radiators and heaters: neither extreme is a good neighbor for a jade, really. Aim for steady daytime temperatures between 60-75°F (16-24°C) and nights around 50-55°F (10-13°C), which keeps growth compact and encourages winter flower buds. You can pick up a digital thermometer to take the guesswork out of it, such as the ThermoPro TP50 Digital Indoor Thermometer, available from Walmart, which can also flag up drafts you might not otherwise notice.

Recent findings suggest that in November, the best thing you can do with your bottle of houseplant fertilizer is tuck it away in a cupboard until spring. Jade plants grow very little in the dark months: feeding them won't change that. They enter a natural dormancy phase during short, low-light winter days, and their roots can’t process the extra nutrients. Feeding a dormant succulent just forces out weak, pale shoots that stretch awkwardly toward the window and snap easily under their own weight.

Industry observers note that unused fertilizer salts can also accumulate rapidly in dry winter potting mix, burning delicate roots and leaving crusty mineral deposits. Whether you tend a classic green jade plant or a trailing Ripple Jade, hold off on all feeding until February. If you did feed in October, that's fine – just don't follow it up! Once bright spring sunlight sparks fresh leaf tips, you can resume feeding every 6-8 weeks through summer. At that point, use a balanced liquid succulent or houseplant fertilizer diluted to half strength.

Warm, dry indoor heating creates prime breeding conditions for sap-sucking houseplant pests, making a thorough inspection essential. Tip your pot gently toward bright window light and check the undersides of leaves and stem junctions. Look for tufts of white fuzz or sticky leaves: these are the telltale signs of citrus mealybugs (Planococcus citri). Any flat, brown, shell-like bumps are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

Quarantine affected plants. Dip a cotton swab in 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol, such as Equate 70% Isopropyl Rubbing Alcohol from Walmart. Dab pests to dissolve their waxy protective coatings, repeating weekly until gone. Keep your jade plant in quarantine for a few weeks. Avoid insecticidal soaps on jade plants. Clemson University’s Home & Garden Information Center warns that fatty-acid soaps can damage jade foliage. While inspecting, pinch off any yellowing lower leaves. Dropping a few older bottom leaves after a fall move is normal. However, dark, mushy stems signal rot, requiring immediate action.

Sources indicate that when a jade plant looks tired in November, resist the urge to try to fix everything at once. You might want to pull it out, give it a latest pot and take the pruners to it, but you need to hold off on this. Roots that get disturbed now don't grow back swiftly, and big pruning cuts made now won't see new growth for months. Save routine repotting and shaping shears for spring, using a fast-draining cactus mix such as Espoma CA4 Organic Cactus Mix, available from Walmart, when the time comes.

Recent findings suggest that the only reason to repot now is if your plant has a rot emergency. If stems feel soft or the pot emits a sour odor, slide the plant out of its pot immediately. Trim away brown, rotted roots and soft stem tissue with sterilized snips. Let the calluses dry for a couple of days, then pot your jade into fresh, dry cactus mix. Hold off on water for a full week afterward. Don't let worry turn into extra watering. Too much water is one of the quickest ways to lose a jade in winter.

Caring for a jade plant in November is less about doing more, and more about stepping back thoughtfully. By scaling back your watering can, moving plants into bright southern light, guarding against chilly windows and drafts, shelving fertilizer, and keeping an eye out for winter pests, your jade will thrive. With a little attention now (and some cool, dark nights on your side), your jade may even reward you with pretty star-shaped winter blooms, before pushing out new leaves in spring.
